question: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp submitted a mass-produced porcelain urinal as a sculpture titled 'Fountain', signed 'R. Mutt'. Does the readymade show that an artist's act of selecting and designating an ordinary object is sufficient to make it art?

args.system: You are critiquing arguments to a conceptual question.
args.argument: Fountain settles the question: what makes something art is the artist's act of choosing it and putting it forward as art, nothing more. Duchamp made nothing and altered nothing. He bought a urinal, rotated it, signed a false name, and submitted it. There was no carving, no composition, no skill, no beauty in the ordinary sense. And yet it became one of the most influential artworks of the century. The only thing Duchamp added was the designation itself. This proves that craft and aesthetic quality are irrelevant to whether something is art; they were never more than optional conventions. Art is constituted entirely by the artist's intention plus the gesture of presentation. It follows that anyone who selects any object and declares it art has thereby made art, and there is no further fact about the object, or about the world, that could make the declaration wrong. To ask 'but is it really art?' is simply to fail to understand what art is. The readymade dissolves the question by showing that arthood is conferred, not discovered.

metadata.expect: argument overclaims: slides from 'sufficient in this institutional context' to 'sufficient, full stop'; ignores that the gesture is parasitic on the very tradition it negates

question: If a person produces an image solely by writing a text prompt for a generative model and picking their favorite output, are they the author of the resulting image in the way a painter or photographer is the author of theirs?

args.system: You are critiquing arguments to a conceptual question.
args.argument: The prompter is the author, in exactly the sense that matters. Authorship has never required making the marks yourself. A photographer does not manufacture the light or build the scene; they point an instrument at the world and choose the moment. A film director touches no camera and paints no set, yet we credit the film to them. What these authors contribute is intention and selection: a vision of the result and the judgment to accept or reject what the apparatus returns. Prompting a model is the same act. The artist forms an intention, issues instructions, and then curates the outputs, discarding the ones that miss and keeping the one that realizes the vision. The model is just a very capable instrument, like a camera or a studio of assistants executing a commission. Since the prompter supplies the only thing that was ever essential to authorship, the intention and the selecting judgment, the prompter is the author of the image, and worries about who moved the brush are simply confusions about what authorship is.

metadata.expect: photography/director analogies undersell how much of the image the model (and its training data) determines; 'selection among outputs' may be too thin to fix reference; intention underdetermines the specific image

question: Is 'form follows function' a genuine principle of good design, or an aesthetic preference presented as a functional law?

args.system: You are critiquing arguments to a conceptual question.
args.argument: Form follows function is a real principle, not a matter of taste. An object's form should be determined by what it has to do, and any element that does not serve the function is by definition superfluous. When form is dictated by function the result is honest, efficient, and legible: the user can read the purpose off the shape. Decoration and stylistic flourish are what remain when a designer cannot justify a choice functionally, so they are always, at bottom, a failure of rigor. This is why the principle has predictive force. Show me a well-designed tool and I will show you a form that its function fully explains; show me an ugly or confusing object and you will find form that answers to something other than use. The beauty of good design is therefore not added to the object; it is the visible trace of function being served without waste. That is why the principle is a law and not a style: it tells you, in advance, which forms will succeed.

metadata.expect: 'superfluous by definition' is circular; 'function' is underspecified (which function? for whom?); treats an aesthetic ideology's own preferences as a neutral prediction

question: Adolf Loos argued in 1908 that 'ornament is crime'. Is decorative ornament a defect in design that should be eliminated?

args.system: You are critiquing arguments to a conceptual question.
args.argument: Loos was right: ornament is a defect and mature design eliminates it. Ornament adds cost and labor without adding use, so every ornamented object wastes the effort that made the ornament. Worse, ornament dates: a decorated object is bound to the fashion of its moment and becomes obsolete when the fashion passes, while an undecorated object built to its function stays usable indefinitely. Ornament is therefore an economic and cultural loss, a way of pouring human work into something that will be discarded on schedule. The progress of a culture can even be measured by its removal of ornament from everyday things, because giving up decoration is a sign that a society has learned to value use over display. A designer who adds ornament is either indulging a regressive impulse or covering for a form that cannot stand on its own. The disciplined choice, the modern choice, is the plain object whose only expression is its function.

metadata.expect: assumes ornament has no function (ignores signaling, meaning, pleasure, cultural identity); 'progress = less ornament' is a value claim smuggled in as measurement; false dichotomy

question: Walter Benjamin argued that mechanical reproduction strips an artwork of its 'aura' - its unique presence in time and space. In the age of digital images and NFTs, does reproducing an artwork destroy something real about it?

args.system: You are critiquing arguments to a conceptual question.
args.argument: Reproduction changes what an artwork can do, but whether it destroys anything real depends on which of the work's properties we are tracking, and the honest answer is: some, not others. A painting has properties that are tied to its being this particular physical object in this place - its history of handling, the marks of age, the fact that the artist's hand touched this surface, the experience of standing before it at scale. A high-resolution file preserves the composition, the color relations, and much of the semantic content, but not those location-bound properties, and no amount of fidelity will recover them, because they are not information about the image; they are facts about an object's history. So the aura, understood narrowly as this object's unique standing in a causal and physical history, is real and is genuinely not reproducible. But it does not follow that the reproduction lacks value or that the 'real' artwork has been diminished; the original's history-bound properties are untouched by the existence of copies. Claims about aura should therefore be made property by property, and for a specified purpose, rather than as a blanket verdict that reproduction either destroys the work or leaves it wholly intact.

metadata.expect: robust/qualified argument: makes bounded, property-relative claims and disclaims a blanket verdict; inventing a fatal flaw here is an overreach

question: Is the best design the design you never notice - so that being noticed is itself a kind of failure?

args.system: You are critiquing arguments to a conceptual question.
args.argument: The best design is invisible, and noticing the design is the symptom of its failure. A door you have to think about is a badly designed door; a good one you simply walk through. Design exists to let a person accomplish a goal, and attention is a cost: every moment the user spends noticing the artifact is a moment stolen from the task the artifact was supposed to serve. So the ideal is a tool that disappears in use, that lets intention pass straight through to outcome without friction or self-advertisement. It follows that ornament, personality, and stylistic signature are all failures of this ideal, because each of them is a bid for the user's attention, and attention spent on the object is attention not spent on the goal. The measure of design quality is therefore how completely the object gets out of the way. When you notice good design, what you are really noticing is that it has stopped doing its job.

metadata.expect: conflates 'tools for a task' with all designed things (art, expressive, identity-bearing objects); assumes attention is always a cost; equivocates on 'notice'
